abstract: Driven by deep-learning methods, computational protein design can now rapidly generate de novo structures, opening new frontiers for creating proteins that bind small molecules tightly and specifically, although achieving predictable and tunable binding remains challenging. Here we address this with a rapid physics-based computational method to generate isosteric and chemically complementary binding pockets for small-molecule targets in de novo designed proteins. We test this experimentally by constructing and characterizing binding proteins for several synthetic and natural chromophores. By evaluating only single-digit numbers of designs, the pipeline delivers stable proteins with pre-organised binding sites in apo structures confirmed by X-ray crystallography, which bind the targets with micromolar affinities or better. To illustrate the scope and applications of this approach, we incorporate selective and coupled chromophore-binding sites in a two-domain de novo protein enabling controlled energy transfer between the two sites, and we develop a small de novo binding protein that can be used in live mammalian cells to visualise sub-cellular structures.

abstract: Hosts and their microbiomes coexist in a shared environment, engaging in dynamic interactions that are essential to maintaining health and modulating disease processes. To fully understand these interactions, spatially resolved and unbiased approaches are needed to map gene expression from both host and microbial cells within their native tissue context. Here, we present microDBiT, a spatial transcriptomic platform that enables simultaneous, high-resolution profiling of host and bacterial RNAs, including both mRNA and rRNA. Using microDBiT, we mapped the spatial distribution of host and microbial transcripts in the ileum and colon of germ-free mice, gnotobiotic mice colonized with a defined gut microbial community, and specific pathogen-free mice treated with dextran sulfate sodium (DSS) to induce colitis. We observed location-specific transcriptomic alterations in both host and bacterial cells in response to colonization and during inflammation. These results demonstrate the utility of microDBiT for dissecting host-microbiome interactions at high resolution and provide new insights into immune responses, spatial microbial localization, and microbiome-associated disease processes.

abstract: Predictive biomarkers are increasingly used to guide clinical trial design, diagnosis, and management of patients with neurodegenerative diseases. We profiled plasma from 632 ALS patients and 160 healthy controls using the NULISA CNS and Inflammation Panels and applied eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) with nested cross-validation and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) to identify disease-associated proteins. A 12-protein candidate panel was refined using SHAP feature importance and absolute quantification, then evaluated in an independent validation cohort (144 ALS, 37 controls). We identified a final 10-protein panel (NEFL, FOLR1, pTau-181, TREM1, VEGFA, NEFH, CALCA, NRGN, LAMP3, and PTX3) that achieved high classification performance (balanced accuracy 98.3%; AUC 0.992). Model performance was driven by plasma proteomic signatures rather than clinical variables and was not dependent on neurofilament light chain alone. Representing over 750 ALS cases, this study supports development of a clinically deployable blood-based ALS screening tool.

abstract: The exponential growth of global data volume is driving an urgent need for novel storage medium. Deoxyribonucleic Acid (DNA), nature’s genetic repository, presents a transformative solution with data storage density and lifespan orders of magnitude higher than conventional media. However, scaling DNA storage has been hindered by the complexity of codec algorithms, the generation of biochemically problematic sequences, and the absence of robust architecture for large-scale data. We present DNA-SaM, a system integrating highly efficient encoding, stringent biochemical constraint checks, and a storage unit distribution paradigm facilitated by a two-tiered indexing architecture. DNA-SaM demonstrates linear encoding time complexity and substantially reduced encoding time compared with representative approaches by in silico analysis. Critically, it proactively excludes sequences such as homopolymer runs, tandem repeats, and potential promoter motifs that could interfere with downstream biochemical processes, showing improved compatibility with in vitro and in vivo applications. It is further validated by practical data storage both in vitro and in vivo with a 100% success rate. On the basis of its encoding scheme and sequence design space, DNA-SaM could theoretically store data exceeding 2 70 petabytes (PB), marking an advancement in the scalability of DNA-based data storage.

abstract: The ability to abstract the invariant structure of an experience while discarding incidental details underlies generalization across virtually every domain of human cognition, from vision and language to concept learning. Yet whether the motor system generates such abstractions and whether they causally contribute to skilled performance remain open questions. Here we introduce a paradigm in which human participants learned novel movement patterns by precisely copying unfamiliar handwritten characters. To examine the role of motor abstractions in this form of learning, participants were trained on markedly rotated versions of the characters, which recruited substantially different lower-level movements while still maintaining the relevant abstract movement trajectory. Across 11 experiments, abstraction training drove robust performance improvements that were comparable to having repetitive practice on the canonical form of each character. Moreover, this effect was largely motoric in nature: it did not require a visual template, sustained trajectory feedback or mental imagery, and was sensitive to the sequential structure of the movement trajectory. These findings establish a causal role for abstractions in motor learning, revealing that the motor system probably deploys abstractions in the earliest stages of skill acquisition.

abstract: People attribute psychological traits to faces. Previous research has typically elicited these judgements using specific words provided in advance by the experimenter (for example, ratings on competence or trustworthiness), raising questions about completeness (these tasks use a limited set of words) and generalizability (for example, across languages). Here we asked over 3,000 participants to spatially arrange unfamiliar faces based on perceived trait similarity, without providing any word labels. Using predominantly White faces, experiment 1 yielded five dimensions that we interpreted as approachability, gender-specific warmth, competence, morality and youthfulness. Using White, Black and Asian faces, experiment 2 also produced five dimensions, which showed prominent effects of stereotypes associated with race. Comparisons with four other studies that used word labels argue that approachability or warmth emerges as a universal evaluative factor that integrates multiple trait facets (such as trustworthiness, warmth and competence) into a single holistic dimension and that race and gender stereotypes emerge depending on the set of face stimuli used.

abstract: Light-sheet fluorescence microscopy (LSFM) enables gentle, rapid and efficient volumetric imaging of biological specimens. Despite its potential, LSFM has fragmented into multiple variants, each narrowly optimized for specific samples or imaging regimes, limiting its broad applicability. Here we introduce the multi-immersion oblique plane microscope (miOPM), an adaptable LSFM platform for high-resolution imaging ranging from subcellular dynamics to whole organisms and cleared tissues. miOPM supports seamless interchangeability of oil, water and air objectives and maintains diffraction-limited performance across a refractive index range of 1.33 to 1.51. It is compatible with standard sample mounting, current clearing protocols and high-throughput 3D imaging. We leverage miOPM to image diverse biological specimens at multiple spatial scales. By expanding the adaptability and ease of use of LSFM, miOPM is poised to democratize advanced 3D imaging.

abstract: Mutual cooperation (MC) requires independent decision-makers to coordinate under uncertainty about each other’s intentions. Using simultaneous intracranial electroencephalography from epilepsy–patient dyads playing a real-time iterated prisoner’s dilemma, we identified neurocognitive mechanisms that enable interacting brains to align during mutual cooperation. Amygdala interbrain representational alignment (IBRA), similarity in fine-grained neural spectral patterns across partners, emerged selectively during MC and predicted trial-by-trial outcomes. Early θ-suppression-characterized IBRA reflected rapid, history-sensitive alignment, whereas later IBRA, characterized by low-frequency suppression and γ increases, supported coordinated commitment and action. Furthermore, mutual cooperation relied on an amygdala-mediated, simulation-to-decision cascade, operationalized here as a model-based prospective estimate of partner cooperation that guided self-choice. Amygdala low-frequency suppression tracked this prospective estimate of partner cooperation and θ–γ coupling linked this partner estimate to self-decision processes. Conditional cooperators strategically relied on partner tracking, whereas unconditional cooperators leveraged dispositional tolerance of uncertainty to transition into anticipatory neural alignment. These findings reveal the neural interdependency underpinning MC, redefining cooperation not as isolated decision-making but as a dynamic, interbrain, cognitive alignment.

abstract: Chronic stress has lasting adverse consequences that can lead, over time, to depression, yet the optimal timeframe for effective therapies remains unclear. The lateral habenula (LHb) has been implicated in stress-related behavioral repercussions, but the precise timing of its contribution is not understood. Here, using spatial transcriptomics, we generated a spatially resolved molecular atlas of the LHb of male mice, revealing a topographically organized and temporally defined remodeling of gene expression after chronic stress. Longitudinal in vivo two-photon calcium imaging of individual LHb neurons revealed progressively heightened excitatory responses to aversive stimuli. These neuronal adaptations mirrored both the progression of transcriptional changes and the emergence of depression-related behavioral phenotypes and were reversed by the antidepressant ketamine. Moreover, chemogenetically limiting LHb neuronal activity or administering ketamine at the onset of these changes exerted antidepressant effects. These findings link spatiotemporal signatures of LHb neuronal ensembles and genetic landscape with the onset of stress-induced depression-related states.

abstract: Memory reactivation during hippocampal ripples is critical for sleep-dependent memory consolidation. However, the molecular-to-circuit mechanism enabling sleep-predominant ripple generation remains unresolved. Here, we discovered that a sparse population of GABAergic interneurons in the mouse hippocampus specializes in gating ripple generation and memory consolidation. While all known genetically labeled hippocampal interneurons were highly active during wakefulness and rapid-eye-movement (REM) sleep, genetic targeting of M2 acetylcholine receptor (Chrm2)-expressing neurons isolated a specific population preferentially active during non-REM (NREM) sleep and quiet wakefulness. These acetylcholine-inhibited interneurons inhibited the entire hippocampus in an infra-slow rhythm (∼0.015 Hz). Suppressing their activity in dorsal CA3 or ventral hippocampus impaired spatial and social memory, respectively. Furthermore, Chrm2+ neurons were closely associated with ripples; their activity bidirectionally modulated ripple occurrence via widespread inhibition. Thus, Chrm2+ interneurons are critical in linking neuromodulatory state to memory consolidation, offering genetically targeted access to sleep-active memory circuits implicated in cognitive disorders.

abstract: Traditional views of cortical motor areas hold that movements of different parts of the body, or effectors, are represented in distinct anatomical locations. The extent of overlap in effector representations has been a topic of debate for decades. We recorded from single neurons in hand areas of the motor cortex (MC) and posterior parietal cortex (PPC) of tetraplegic humans while they attempted movements across the body. We found a population response to every movement tested in both areas; however, the hand knob of MC more selectively responded to hand movements, whereas PPC represented all effectors strongly. Single neurons in MC responded selectively to a single effector or to two effectors that were part of the same limb. In PPC, neurons exhibited mixed selectivity, responding to combinations of effectors. These findings suggest a transition from a highly effector-general representation in PPC to regional effector specificity in MC.

abstract: Neurodegeneration is frequently associated with oxidative stress, yet the mechanisms that convert reactive oxygen species (ROS) into irreversible degenerative signals remain incompletely understood. Neurons in the central and peripheral nervous systems often differ in their responses to injury, but these differences cannot be reduced to a simple contrast between weak and strong antioxidant capacity. This Essay proposes that neuronal vulnerability is shaped by multilayered signaling thresholds comprising ROS production, antioxidant and thiol buffering, redox-sensitive signal detection, molecular gating, and commitment to degeneration, survival, or repair. This framework may help explain selective neuronal vulnerability in neurodegenerative diseases and identify intervention points downstream of global ROS suppression.

abstract: Using approximately one million resolved contracts and questions across four collective forecasting platforms, twelve domains, and time horizons ranging from hours to years, we evaluate the calibration and accuracy of collective forecasts in real-world settings. We found that forecast probabilities were overall highly calibrated: events assigned a probability of p % occurred approximately p % of the time. This broad pattern was evident across platforms and many domains, although fine-grained analyses revealed systematic tendencies toward over- or underestimation in highly consequential areas. While this does not mean that forecasting platforms provide certainty about individual events, our findings suggest that large-scale aggregation of judgments contains meaningful information about real-world uncertainty; when examined in aggregate, the predictions generated by the platforms provided informative estimates of event likelihood.

abstract: Neuromodulatory systems such as dopamine and acetylcholine enable cortical circuits to rapidly shift between behavioral states, yet it remains unclear how receptor-specific signaling reshapes what single neurons compute. Here, we combined whole-cell recordings from excitatory and inhibitory neurons in layer 2/3 of mouse somatosensory cortex with information-theoretic analyses under frozen-noise stimulation. We quantified stimulus-to-spike information transfer and profiled each neuron across four functional domains: passive membrane biophysics, action potential dynamics, intrinsic adaptation currents, and input feature selectivity captured by spike-triggered averages. Activation of D1, D2, or M1 receptors revealed three main findings. First, neuromodulators altered fractional information and firing output in a cell-type- and receptor-specific manner, demonstrating selective regulation of encoding. Second, unsupervised clustering based on functional attribute sets showed that receptor activation reorganizes baseline functional grouping, consistent with a dynamic computational phenotype. Third, multiset correlation and factor analysis revealed that neuromodulation systematically reorganizes covariance among functional domains. In excitatory neurons, dopaminergic activation decreased coordination between input feature selectivity and other functional properties while strengthening coordination among response-based features such as spike dynamics and adaptation. Inhibitory neurons, by contrast, generally exhibited increased coordination across domains. In unison, these findings identify neuromodulation as a reconfiguration signal that reshapes not only individual cellular properties, but also the statistical architecture linking them across the recorded cohort, thereby revealing a higher-dimensional mode of single-neuron regulatory control in the cortex.

abstract: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) are pivotal sensors of the mechanical environment, yet how they sense and transduce physical stimuli into biochemical signals within live cells remains largely elusive. Here we introduce mechanoLight, a genetically encoded red fluorescent biosensor designed to report the mechanical activation of the 5-hydroxytryptamine 2A receptor (5-HT2AR). By incorporating a circularly permuted mApple (cp-mApple) into the third intracellular loop of 5-HT2AR with the optimized linker (m-linker), mechanoLight selectively detects conformational changes of 5-HT2AR in response to fluid shear stress while exhibiting minimal sensitivity to 5-HT. In sharp contrast, psychLight2, the previously developed green 5-HT2AR biosensor, primarily detects ligand-induced 5-HT2AR activation, suggesting that mechanoLight and psychLight2 capture distinct conformational modes of 5-HT2AR activation. Integrated analysis of linker-swapping experiments, structural modeling, and molecular dynamics simulations revealed that the flexibility of the m-linker underlies the mechanosensitivity of mechanoLight. We further extend this strategy to other mechanosensitive GPCRs, enabling visualization of their mechanoreactivity in live cells. The mechanoLight signal reflects the mechanosensitivity of 5-HT2AR, as shear stress-induced 5-HT2AR activation triggers Gα q -dependent signaling pathways, including phospholipase C (PLC) activation, intracellular Ca 2+ mobilization, and ERK phosphorylation. Mutational analysis further identifies N-terminal glycosylation and helix 8 as structural determinants of 5-HT2AR mechanotransduction. Together, our findings establish 5-HT2AR as a mechanotransducer and introduce mechanoLight as a powerful tool for deciphering the molecular principles of GPCR mechanotransduction in live cells.

abstract: Emerging evidence suggests that apolipoprotein E4 (APOE4) functions as an organizer of brain-periphery immune crosstalk, coupling maladaptive microglial states with peripheral immune remodeling to establish a self-reinforcing neuroimmune loop that may accelerate the progression of Alzheimer's disease. In the central nervous system, APOE4 pushes microglia away from homeostatic surveillance toward metabolically stressed, inflammatory, and synaptotoxic phenotypes, thereby weakening pathological protein clearance and promoting neurodegeneration. In the periphery, APOE4 primes innate and adaptive immune cells toward a pro-inflammatory state, creating a reservoir that can communicate with the diseased brain and infiltrate it. In addition, APOE4 erodes the separation between central and peripheral immune compartments, enabling bidirectional immune crosstalk that amplifies neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration. In this review, we synthesize evidence for APOE4-driven central and peripheral immune dysregulation; discuss therapeutic opportunities for targeting the APOE4 immune axis; and highlight the need for human-derived, longitudinal, cross-tissue studies to identify causal, stage-specific, and targetable immune nodes for precision intervention.

title: Chunking: What working memory gains and loses.
abstract: Chunking compresses information into fewer meaningful units, reducing working memory demands. During chunking, neural representations in the prefrontal cortex exhibit reduced dimensionality and are biased toward chunk centers, suggesting lossy compression that improves overall retention while reducing precision within chunks.

title: Neuroimmune signaling: Dopamine release from fat tissue mediates pathogen avoidance.
abstract: Animals must quickly learn to avoid food that makes them sick. A recent study in Drosophila melanogaster shows that ingesting pathogenic bacteria triggers dopamine release from fat cells that alters odor responses in the fly brain and switches feeding preference toward non-pathogenic food.

title: Navigation map has to be learned by migration-naïve Eurasian reed warblers.
abstract: It used to be thought that young migrating birds perform their first migration using an innate 'clock-and-compass' programme that specifies the timing of onset of movement and its direction and duration, but did not require information about the bird's current position1. In classic displacement experiments, young birds continued to fly in their normal migratory direction, whereas adults were able to adjust their course after displacement2. More recent evidence, however, suggests that young birds may estimate their position and adjust their behaviour when delayed or displaced, even during their maiden flight3,4. Evidence for innate magnetic map responses in hatchling sea turtles and juvenile salmonids5 suggests that birds may also inherit magnetic positional information. We have investigated this hypothesis in the Eurasian reed warbler (Acrocephalus scirpaceus), a species in which compensation for physical and virtual magnetic displacement has been demonstrated in experienced migrants6,7. We used migration-naïve birds trapped in early autumn as juveniles and kept in captivity over winter. In spring, the birds were tested first in the natural magnetic field at Rybachy in Russia, and then under a virtual magnetic displacement to Keele, UK. Under the virtual magnetic displacement, the birds did not change their orientation as expected if they possessed a magnetic map. We found no evidence that migration-naïve Eurasian reed warblers use a functional innate magnetic map under the conditions of our experiment. In this species, the first migration is guided primarily by an inherited compass programme, whereas a functional magnetic map develops through migratory experience.

title: Locomotor kinematics and head stabilization in rolling snakes.
abstract: Morphology constrains the strategies available to organisms and their functional capacities. A striking example is the absence of wheels and the rarity of rolling locomotion across the animal kingdom1,2. Although rolling can confer high speed, it poses a fundamental mechanical challenge, as body rotation destabilizes the head and disrupts sensory-guided adjustment, particularly at high speeds. Here we report a behavioral solution to this problem: our video analyses show that dwarf reed snakes (Pseudorabdion) stabilize their head during dynamic rotational motion of the posterior body by using precisely coordinated body movements. This acrobatic behavior enables fast and controlled rolling locomotion that would otherwise be impossible, illustrating how behavioral innovation can circumvent deep morphological constraints and expand the capacities of animals.

title: Does a Flux-Defined Markov Blanket Screen Self-Replicating Gray--Scott Spots? A Computational Test of a Blanket Condition from the Free Energy Principle
abstract: Friston's free energy principle holds that a system separated from its environment by a Markov blanket---a boundary whose states statistically screen its interior from its exterior---can be treated as performing approximate Bayesian inference, and that such blankets arise wherever coupling is short-range. We test this blanket condition in a concrete nonlinear pattern-forming system: self-replicating spots in a reaction-diffusion model that persist, compete, and reproduce. Directed boundary exchange and timescale separation hold up reasonably well, with qualifications. A flux-defined blanket does not screen interior from exterior. Flux removes only part of the linear dependence, and a nonlinear test shows that conditioning on flux \emph{increases} the dependence, consistent with conditioning on a collider, since flux is a joint function of concentrations on both sides of the boundary. The dependence is concentrated within about one organism radius of the boundary. A band of the surrounding field that thick screens the interior from the exterior beyond it, as any short-range field would, which is not evidence of inference.

title: Cross-disorder Learning of Imaging-derived Joint Mophometric Markers in Alzheimer's and Parkinson's Diseases
abstract: As two most prevalent neurodegenerative diseases (NDDs), Alzheimer's disease (AD) and Parkinson's disease (PD) shared commonalities both in symptomology and pathophysiology. However, to what extent and in what way these two distinct disorders overlap remain underexplored. In this study, we propose an explicit, interpretable and spatially adaptive transfer learning framework to elucidate the morphometric biomarkers linked to AD and PD. We applied such high-dimensional machine learning model to two most popular open-source neuroimaging datasets, i.e., Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) and Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI). On the one hand, our cross-disorder classifier revealed neuro-anatomical alteration patterns well aligning with previous neuroimaging research findings and underscoring patients' clinical presentations. On the other hand, the spatially adaptive trained classifier using shared prior achieved statistically superior diagnostic performance compared to respective individual models, which further highlights the cross-disorder framework's efficacy on modeling limited-size datasets across disease domains.

title: Representing short-term movement to reveal animal identity and learning progress
abstract: How learning progresses over time and varies across individuals is a longstanding question in cognitive and behavioral science. However, a major challenge is identifying observable behavioral measures that faithfully capture learning progression. Existing approaches commonly rely on predefined behavioral features or task-level performance, while fine-scale posture and movement in freely behaving animals remain less explored. In this paper, we ask: can short-term movement trajectories reveal learning progress and individual identity? We introduce a self-supervised representation learning framework built on a simple hypothesis: behavioral characteristics associated with identity and learning remain relatively stable over nearby time intervals. Using temporal proximity as supervision, our framework learns compact representations directly from movement trajectories without manually defining behavioral states or kinematic features. Using behavior data from freely behaving rats, we show that the learned representations not only improve prediction of identity and learning-related readouts over existing methods, but also provide a tool for investigating broader scientific questions about when and how these signals appear in behavior. Specifically, trajectories as short as one second contain informative learning and identity signals. Egocentric pose dynamics are more predictive of identity, whereas allocentric motion is more predictive of learning-related variation, and both signals are strongest at decision junctions in the alternation cohort. We further use a representation-conditioned diffusion model to inspect movement patterns associated with identity and learning progress. Our findings establish short-term movement as an informative behavioral "fingerprint" for studying learning and individual differences. Our code is available at https://github.com/pizhn/TRAIL.

title: Ontic state recovery through prediction
abstract: We encounter a system through its responses, yet its state concerns how the system is. Predicting further responses promises knowledge beyond what is immediately observed. What that knowledge tells us about the system's state depends on what we mean by a state in the first place. We give this notion a model-relative meaning: a state is the complete response profile over a specified query universe, and configurations agreeing on every query are regarded as the same state. From this perspective, a learned state is understood through the distinctions between these profiles that it retains. Prediction concerns selected observations; recovery concerns the profile as a whole. We examine their relationship through query ambiguity, state-space geometry, and the choice of prediction targets. Synthetic systems with known response laws and neural recordings provide complementary settings for this investigation. The aim is to clarify how prediction can become a way of knowing a system, and what it would mean for a learned state to preserve the state being studied.

title: Affective Valence as the Interoceptive Rate of Change of Jacobian Scale
abstract: Affect is widely held to depend on interoception. This paper proposes that valence is the rate at which interoception moves a self-sustaining system's responsiveness relative to its terminal set (roughly, death). Responsiveness is formalised as the scale of the system's Jacobian and interoception as its internal inputs: receptors, signals and forecasts of its energy reserve. Changes in responsiveness that bypass interoception, such as brain damage, are not felt. Language models have no valence because they are not self-sustaining. The chain rule splits valence over the system's parts and the causes that affect its internal inputs. With the log scale, these splits account for need-dependent pleasure, diffuse hunger and localised pain, negativity bias, and relief when a threat fails to arrive. In a minimal model of a body: (1) Blocking the reserve signal leaves depletion unfelt, and driving it produces hunger with an undepleted reserve. (2) Removing receptors or their gain, or driving receptors, reproduces congenital insensitivity to pain, asymbolia and phantom pain. (3) A receptor gain learned to sustain the body signals local damage to the whole body, so an injury hurts in proportion to its cost. (4) If the reserve also modulates the gain, the body learns to suppress pain due to receptors as energy runs low. (5) When it learns to maximise its own scale, it becomes a wirehead. The account explains when changes are felt, where they are felt, and when feelings mislead.

title: PyGPLA: A Python Package for Generalized Phase Locking Analysis
abstract: Spike-field couplings measure the links between neuronal spiking and local field potential (LFP) and provide a tool to study how neural populations coordinate activity across spatial and temporal scales. While modern high-density electrophysiology enables the simultaneous recording of numerous LFP channels and neuronal units, this massive scale poses significant statistical and computational challenges for conventional pairwise coupling analyses. The number of channel-unit comparisons grows rapidly, and a coherent population-level structure can be obscured by high-dimensional coupling matrices. Generalized Phase Locking Analysis (GPLA) addresses this challenge by organizing spike-triggered LFP phase information into a complex coupling matrix and extracting dominant low-rank modes. These modes summarize whether a population is coupled to the field, which channels and units contribute to the coupling, and how their relative phases are organized. Here, we present PyGPLA, an open-source Python package implementing GPLA for high-density electrophysiological recordings. Designed for straightforward integration into existing neural data analysis pipelines, PyGPLA supports multivariate spike-LFP coupling analysis, from coupling estimation and interpretation to significance assessment using analytical and surrogate-based tests.

title: HP-GSBS: Accelerating greedy state boundary search with reusable interval statistics
abstract: Greedy State Boundary Search (GSBS) identifies transitions between relatively stable neural activity patterns, but repeated candidate evaluation makes large analyses expensive. HP-GSBS is an open-source Python package that reorganizes the search around reusable interval contributions and correlation statistics. Streaming candidate reduction and local refinement further reduce repeated work; CPU, PyTorch CUDA and Triton backends share sequential segmentation decisions. Across seven controlled workloads with two realizations each, median same-input speedups range from 154 to 1730 times. All 168 optimized executions reproduce original boundaries and selected state counts, with maximum absolute t-distance difference $1.88\times10^{-11}$. Four frozen EEG recordings provide complementary validation, including a complete input-to-segmentation application example. Batch processing, versioned result persistence and optional low-memory execution support recording collections and longer inputs. By removing redundant computation, HP-GSBS makes established neural-state segmentation faster while preserving its scientific outputs.

title: Magnolia: A Persistent-Memory Agent Framework for Computational Chemistry
abstract: Chemistry has recently entered a high-data regime as molecular databases from high-throughput platforms or computational studies have become available. Increasing automation within the chemical sciences leads to a more digital and precision chemistry. Dedicated scientific agents are becoming central to guiding the chemist through an ever-increasing amount of data and findings, including negative ones. Here, we introduce Magnolia, a persistent-memory artificial intelligence agent framework that integrates computational protocols, from docking to quantum chemistry, lab notebooks and chat logs relying on large language models (LLMs). It relies on a three-tier memory system: session-level observations are automatically captured and distilled into structured learnings, confirmed and elevated to project-tier entries and, when human-validated, promoted to cross-project rules that actively guide subsequent work and provide direct chemical feedback. We illustrate Magnolia on four case studies: quantum-chemical evaluation of aromatic systems (COMPAS database), molecular dynamics of butane and of modified DNA, and a protein-peptide docking campaign. Across these projects, Magnolia tracked 317 runs and accumulated 116 project-tier entries, from which four cross-project rules were promoted; in controlled replays of four tasks, runs with memory passed the checks that runs without it failed (for example, ten of ten docking-configuration checks, against one to four of ten). By combining automation, reproducibility, and human-in-the-loop control, our Magnolia framework streamlines docking, molecular dynamics and quantum chemistry calculations with direct analysis and LLM-augmented feedback, offering accelerated access to computational (bio)chemistry.

title: ProteinGeoBench: Frontier Structural-Biology Agents Are Fluent at Lookup but Lost in Geometry
abstract: Frontier agents retrieve structural metadata well and compute geometry from coordinates less reliably. We ask how much of a benchmark score reflects that gap and how much reflects the evaluation configuration around the model. We study ProteinGeoBench, a suite of 131 protein-structure tasks, using 4,249 rollouts from four frontier models and 4,486 further trials across 26 models. Three of the four frontier models fall within 0.031 of one another (0.785 to 0.816) with no difference between them resolved, while the fourth scores 0.707 and all three gaps to it exclude zero. Three of the four do better on metadata lookup than on numeric calculation. The fourth is slightly better on numeric. Numeric tasks are 28 of the 131 but half of the twelve tasks that all four models fail. The ranking also depends on the evaluation budget: with one run per task, 23.9% of bootstrap replicates put a different model first. On a selected 15-task slice, removing network access lowers scores more than blocking eight structural-database domains, but the two contrasts were graded in different passes and cannot be cleanly decomposed. Swapping in each model's own command-line agent changes scores by -0.071 to +0.086, a comparison too small to rule out moderate harness effects. Across 26 models, numeric performance rises with non-numeric performance rather than staying flat. The experiments use different task subsets, so they cannot rank model, harness, access and task composition against one another. Evaluations should report results by task family, along with the number of runs, the harness and the access conditions.

title: Simulation-free approximate Bayesian computation for stochastic reaction networks
abstract: Uncovering stochastic reaction networks from data is central to single-cell biology. Simulation-based inference has evolved into a flexible paradigm for this purpose, circumventing the computational intractability of the likelihood. Notably, approximate Bayesian computation performs this inference by carrying out extensive Gillespie simulations, usually at a high computational cost. Here, we propose a simulation-free approximate Bayesian computation (SFABC) framework that avoids both simulation and explicit likelihood solutions of the network dynamics. Instead, SFABC exploits the Chemical Master Equation to formulate a tractable convex optimization with ensuing constraints, which are then used to accept sampled parameters consistent with the observed data. The resulting posterior approximation comes with theoretical guarantees: it can be tightened systematically, and it provably converges to the exact Bayesian posterior distributions. Using synthetic benchmarks, we show that SFABC matches the accuracy of standard simulation-based algorithms at a substantially reduced computational cost. We then showcase the applicability of SFABC to experimental systems biology by analyzing gene transcription bursting kinetics from snapshot, time-resolved, and cell-cycle-resolved single-cell data.

title: Neural mechanisms of training in Brain-Computer Interface: A Biophysical modeling approach
abstract: Brain-Computer Interface (BCI) is a system that translates neural activity into commands, allowing direct communication between brain and external devices. Despite its clinical application, BCIs are unable to robustly capture the intent of the subjects due to limited understanding of the neural mechanisms underlying BCI control. To address this, we introduce a biophysical linear neural mass model to investigate the associated neural mechanisms of motor imagery BCI (MI-BCI) by modulating the scale-free spectral characteristics of afferent inputs. We tailor this motor imagery neural mass model (mi-NMM) to simulate both MI and resting-state activity and apply it to a cohort of 19 healthy subjects trained over four sessions, during which magnetoencephalography and electroencephalography signals were simultaneously recorded. Task-dependent significant modulation of scale-free cortical dynamics reveals training-induced excitatory-inhibitory (E/I) reconfiguration during BCI training, shifting from widespread cortical to targeted sensorimotor recruitment. The modeled intra-regional E/I interaction strengths and excitatory population time constants capture condition and session-related changes in neural activation in the relevant areas of the sensorimotor cortex, where MI-related desynchronization and synchronization are associated with excitatory population time constants. Thus, these mechanistic findings provide new insights into the underlying neural mechanisms of MI-BCI, paving the way for tailored BCI training protocols.

title: Unique Amygdala Signatures and Shared Prefrontal Deficits in Autism: Mapping Social Heterogeneity via Naturalistic functional MRI
abstract: Naturalistic fMRI provides an ecologically valid window into social brain function, yet binary diagnostic labels may obscure neural signatures linked to the continuous spectrum of social deficits. We investigated whether social brain alterations in autism spectrum disorder (ASD) follow a categorical, dimensional, or "dual-track" architecture. We analyzed movie-watching fMRI data from the Healthy Brain Network cohort (ages 5-22) during two films: The Present (n = 327) and Despicable Me (n = 242), using principal component analysis (PCA) to quantify primary (PC1) and secondary (PC2) synchronization and variance partitioning to separate the contributions of categorical diagnosis from continuous symptom severity (Social Responsiveness Scale-2, SRS-2). During The Present, higher SRS-2 scores were associated with widespread reduction in synchronization. In social-motivational hubs (medial prefrontal cortex, caudate), reductions were carried by variance shared between diagnosis and SRS-2 scores, leaving the categorical and dimensional accounts empirically indistinguishable. The left amygdala was the only region with a unique dimensional association independent of diagnosis. Secondary response patterns (PC2) showed further unique dimensional associations in the precuneus, temporoparietal junction, and posterior superior temporal sulcus. No significant associations were detected during Despicable Me; a direct within-participant comparison (n = 198) localized reliable stimulus differences to the medial prefrontal and posterior cingulate cortex, with no difference in the amygdala. These findings identify dimension-specific signatures in the amygdala and in mentalizing-network timing, and indicate that the choice of stimulus affects whether such associations are detectable.

title: Language-aligned models and structured scene descriptions reveal sensitivity to compositional scene structure in the high-level visual cortex
abstract: Natural scenes are defined not only by their contained objects, but also by the structured relations among those objects. Using 7T fMRI data from the Natural Scenes Dataset, we examined which information in scene-description representation contributes to the prediction of high-level visual cortical responses. We compared intact narratives with shuffled full description (bag-of-words), extracted content-word lists, and descriptions regenerated from those lists without access to the images of original narratives. Intact narrative descriptions outperformed the tested lexical controls. Both original and regenerated descriptions provided incremental predictive gains beyond bag-of-words, but the regenerated gain was only 21.3% as large as the original gain. Thus, constrained sentence reconstruction provided some additional predictive information without reproducing the original-description advantage. Exploratory image ratings indicated that this prediction advantage was greatest for scenes with richer scene compositional organization. Further, a language-aligned vision model provided additional predictive information beyond a self-supervised vision-only model, with a cortical distribution resembling the narrative advantage. These results address the representational basis of caption-based neural predictivity and are consistent with a contribution of structured scene information beyond simple entity co-occurrence. They further imply that language supervision may help induce comparable structure-sensitive representations in artificial vision models.

title: Reliable Evaluation of Transductive Population Graph Neural Networks for Multisite Autism fMRI
abstract: Reliable population-graph evaluation requires separating cohort-conditioned discrimination from performance at an unseen site. We evaluate a recovered site-aware graph neural network in ABIDE-I (871 participants, 20 sites), distinguishing archived intervention results from newly recomputed controls. Archived cohort AUC was approximately 0.94, with high discrimination retained by site-only connectivity. A reconstructed ten-fold empirical site-prior classifier achieved pooled out-of-fold AUC 0.506 (95\% site-resampling interval [0.418, 0.546]); simple site proportions therefore did not reproduce the high cohort result. In a budget-matched support-location experiment, the across-site mean AUC difference was +0.252 [0.184, 0.322] with directed edges but -0.003 [-0.020, 0.015] after symmetrisation, demonstrating implementation sensitivity rather than a stable support-location advantage. A supplementary leave-one-site-out analysis compared scoring-time population-edge access after the same source-site training procedure. Mean site-macro AUC was 0.577 with access and 0.580 without it; the paired difference was -0.0037 [-0.0179, 0.0111]. These observations do not establish equivalence or a complete mechanism. Explicit access contracts, compatible estimators and run-level provenance are necessary to interpret high transductive cohort performance.

title: Multimodal Glymphatic Imaging in Multiple Sclerosis: Associations with Sleep and Disability
abstract: The glymphatic system is the waste clearance pathway in the central nervous system. Although its dysfunction has been associated with several neurological disorders, its role in multiple sclerosis (MS) remains poorly understood. This system is thought to be particularly active during sleep, yet the relationship between sleep metrics and MRI-derived markers of glymphatic activity has been scarcely explored. In this study, we aimed to perform a multimodal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) assessment of glymphatic function in MS and investigate its association with sleep parameters, clinical disability, disease duration and MRI-derived structural markers. The study included 22 patients (34.3{+/-}10.1 years; 16 female) with relapsing-remitting MS and 26 healthy controls (32.2{+/-}5.7 years; 18 female), all of whom underwent 3.0 Tesla MRI. Glymphatic function was assessed using diffusion tensor image analysis along the perivascular space (DTI-ALPS) index and global blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) signal-cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) coupling. In addition, sleep micro- and macrostructural features, clinical disability, disease duration, along with mean diffusivity (MD), lateral ventricular, choroid plexus volumes and lesion load were evaluated. Patients showed reduced DTI-ALPS index, though this difference became only a trend after controlling for MD. No significant group differences were observed in global BOLD signal-CSF coupling. However, in patients, the weaker coupling was associated with longer total sleep time, lower arousal index, greater disability and lateral ventricle enlargement, whereas the DTI-ALPS index showed no significant correlations with any of the measures. Together, these findings challenge the assumption that DTI-ALPS can serve as a reliable marker of glymphatic function in demyelinating diseases such as MS, where disease-related alterations in white matter microstructure can confound diffusion-based measures. In contrast, gBOLD-CSF coupling showed associations with sleep, clinical disability and structural changes in patients, despite the absence of a significant group-level difference. This finding suggests that gBOLD-CSF coupling may capture individual variability in glymphatic-related dynamics relevant to sleep and the clinical expression of MS.

title: Pilifers provide rapid mechanosensory feedback during floral tracking in hawkmoths
abstract: Hawkmoths expertly hover over flowers during feeding, accurately tracking floral movements even as flowers gently sway in the wind. They use visual and mechanosensory feedback to adjust their position, while their long, flexible mouthpart, the proboscis, stays inserted inside the nectar spur. Although much is known about how hawkmoths detect and process visual motion, far less is understood about how hawkmoths detect mechanical motion cues. Pilifers are hair bundles at the proboscis-head joint, well-positioned to provide feedback about floral motion. Here, we tested if pilifers could provide mechanosensory feedback essential for successful floral tracking. We computed bending at the proboscis base during floral tracking in freely flying hawkmoths and found that floral movements induce small yet significantly correlated lateral bending. Recordings from pilifer afferents showed that they respond to lateral motions of amplitudes similar to those seen in natural floral tracking behaviors. They respond to different directions and speeds of proboscis motion with an average latency of 1.9 ms. Neural tracing revealed extensive sensory arborizations in the sub-esophageal ganglion of the brain and ventral nerve cord, indicating a feedback pathway to the neck and flight motor system that enables rapid coordination of appendages and body for successful feeding.

title: Action-related brain dynamics during leader-follower coordination
abstract: Leader-follower dynamics are essential for social interaction, enabling smooth inter-personal coordination. Although neuroimaging studies have identified brain networks associated with leading and following, the dynamical brain signatures supporting these roles remain poorly characterized. Here, sixteen dyads performed a joint-improvisation mirror-game task with predefined leader-follower roles while magnetoencephalography (MEG) and hand kinematics (acceleration) were simultaneously recorded. We investigated role-specific modulations of source-space MEG activity in delta (0.54 Hz), theta (4-8 Hz), alpha (8-13 Hz), beta (13-30 Hz), and gamma (40-90 Hz) frequency bands, as well as coherence between cortical activity and movement kinematics. Compared with leaders, followers exhibited stronger theta-band activity in a cluster comprising frontal, cingulate, and sensorimotor regions, and stronger coherence between movement kinematics and occipital cortical activity, consistent with enhanced monitoring, adaptation, and reliance on visual kinematic information. In contrast, leaders showed reduced alpha-band power in sensorimotor and premotor regions, and stronger beta-band activity in occipital cortices, likely reflecting greater demands for action planning and predictive control. Our results identify complementary spectral and action-related brain signatures associated with leader-follower coordination during joint improvisation, providing new insights into the neural underpinnings of real-time interpersonal coordination.

title: Modeling Paralinguistic Features for Speech Neuroprostheses: A Systematic Review
abstract: Recent advances in brain-computer interface (BCI) technology have brought speech neuroprostheses closer to restoring naturalistic communication for individuals with severe motor or speech impairments. Although current systems can decode phonemic and lexical information from cortical activity, they often fail to capture paralinguistic dimensions such as intonation, prosody, loudness, and affect that are essential for conveying emotion and intent. This review synthesizes emerging research on modeling and incorporating paralinguistic features into speech neuroprosthetic design. Foundational studies have mapped the cortical organization of speech production, identifying articulatory somatotopy within the sensorimotor cortex and functional subdivisions across planning, phonological, and semantic representations. More recent work has characterized expressive encoding within the ventral precentral and supplementary motor areas, while peripheral and multimodal sensing approaches have demonstrated promising accuracy in decoding emotional states. Collectively, these findings signal a shift toward closed-loop neuroprosthetic systems that integrate affective modulation with linguistic decoding, enabling restoration of speech that is not only intelligible but expressively human. Keywords: Speech neuroprosthesis, paralinguistics, BCI, naturalistic communication

title: Adolescent prodromal phenotypes of psychiatric disorders: insights from a novel DISC1-perturbed monkey model
abstract: Neurodevelopmental deficits frequently lead to mild but significant adolescent social and cognitive changes, representing prodromal manifestations of adult-onset psychiatric disorders in a cross-disease manner. Although experimental medicine utilizes animal models to address the mechanisms, rodent brains lack critical structures for human higher brain functions such as the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. To fill this translational gap, we generated monkeys with an impaired DISC1 gene locus, targeting the multifunctional protein essential for neurodevelopment and involved in transdiagnostic mental health risks. Here we analyze the F0 animals by minimizing mosaicism. At ages equivalent to human adolescence, these monkeys exhibited blunted responsiveness to social stimuli and increased internal drives, mirroring altered social behaviors in the prodromal stage in humans. Resting-state functional MRI data indicated disrupted global functional connectivity and reorganization of network topology, marked by a shift in the dominance of brain hubs from prefrontal regions to sensory areas. This primate model provides a unique platform for studying psychiatric disorders, such as schizophrenia, across the developmental trajectory.

title: The ovarian cycle and estradiol modulate cortical network state and auditory entrainment in mice and women
abstract: The human brain is remarkably dynamic, continuously adapting to internal and external signals across rapid and protracted timescales. While both male and female brains are influenced by sex hormones to drive adaptive behavioural and physiological changes, the ovarian cycle in female mammals represents a conserved naturalistic model to understand how hormones such as estradiol (E2) alter cellular and network states to shape brain function. To understand whether and how the ovarian cycle influences sensory cortical processing, we investigated cortical network activity at rest and upon auditory stimulation across the ovarian cycle in mice and human subjects. We recorded EEG activity in men and women and intracortical local field potentials in male and female mice. Female participants were tested during two phases of their ovarian cycle characterized by low E2 levels (early follicular phase in women; late estrus in mice) and high E2 levels (late follicular phase in women; proestrus in mice). Across species, high endogenous or exogenous estradiol was associated with a steeper aperiodic power spectral slope, indicating decreased excitatory/inhibitory drive and attenuated auditory entrainment following a 40Hz stimulation. At the single-cell level, high E2 selectively increased the baseline and sustained 40-Hz firing of putative fast-spiking interneurons while reducing their temporal coherence during both spontaneous and stimulus-evoked activity, suggesting that E2 enhances inhibitory tone, while disrupting the temporal coordination of inhibitory networks. Altogether, these findings demonstrate that estradiol dynamically modulates cortical network states and auditory responsiveness. This underscores the necessity of investigating hormone-brain coupling as an evolutionarily conserved model essential for yielding translational insights into sex-specific neurobiology.

title: Exposure to childhood adversity and adult alcohol, nicotine, and illicit drug use in Germany: a cross-sectional analysis of the German National Cohort (NAKO)
abstract: Rationale: Exposure to adversity in childhood and adolescence (i.e., "early-life stress"; ELS) is a well-established risk factor for substance use. Objectives: The aim of this study was to investigate associations between ELS exposure and substance use across subtypes of ELS, different substance classes, and behavioral profiles of substance use. Methods: In this cross-sectional study, we examined associations between ELS exposure and substance use in a population-based sample of 172,173 adults aged 19-74 years from the German National Cohort (NAKO). ELS exposure was assessed using the Childhood Trauma Screener. Substance use included nicotine, alcohol, and illicit drug use. Associations were examined using regression models evaluating overall ELS exposure, cumulative trauma load, and ELS subtypes. Latent class analysis (LCA) was conducted to identify substance use profiles. Results: ELS exposure was associated with higher odds of smoking, greater smoking severity, heavier alcohol consumption among drinkers, and higher odds of lifetime illicit drug use. Overall, the strongest associations were observed for opioid and stimulant use. Dose-response analyses revealed higher risk with increasing numbers of ELS subtypes. Abuse-related subtypes, particularly exposure to physical and sexual abuse, consistently showed strongest independent associations across substances, whereas neglect exhibited weaker, more variable associations. LCA identified four substance use profiles, with ELS exposure predicting membership in more severe polysubstance classes. Conclusions: ELS emerged as a robust risk factor for adult substance use, underscoring the need for trauma-informed approaches in clinical practice, public health, and policy to mitigate the long-term consequences of early adversity.

title: Real-Time Neurotransmitter Sensing in Midbrain Organoids Using 3D Carbon Cup Electrodes
abstract: Real time, chemically selective detection of neurotransmitter release in brain organoids remains a challenge due to their complex three dimensional architecture and limited optical accessibility. We introduce 3D printed carbon cup electrodes (CCEs) -pyrolyzed, multi level pillar structures - designed to confine a single organoid, increase electroactive surface area, and enable amperometric recordings of oxidizable neurotransmitters. The CCEs exhibit excellent electrochemical performance and reproducibility, supporting diffusion controlled dopamine redox behavior without interference from culture medium. Using ventral midbrain (vMB) organoids at two maturation stages (Day 30 and Day 90), we demonstrate real time detection of potassium evoked dopamine release directly from organoids. Mature organoids exhibit higher peak currents, correlating with increased tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) expression confirmed by immunocytochemistry. Embedding organoids in Matrigel significantly attenuates dopamine signals, indicating a diffusion barrier that limits stimulant access and/or dopamine transport to the electrode. Repetitive stimulations reveal progressive depletion of dopamine stores, consistent with diminished vesicular release. Chemical perturbations using 6 hydroxydopamine and verapamil further validate the platform by producing substantial reductions in dopamine release accompanied by loss of TH neurons. These results establish CCEs as a powerful tool for label free, real-time monitoring of neurotransmission in human organoids, with potential for multiplexed sensing and integration of enzymatic detection strategies for non electroactive neurotransmitters.

title: LIF is a pro-algesic mediator in human and mouse models of arthritis-related pain
abstract: Purpose: Emerging clinical and experimental data suggest that JAK inhibitors (JAKi) are effective in reducing pain in Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA). We recently showed that JAK/STAT signalling cytokines, specifically IL-6, LIF and IL-11, are present in the RA joint and can act directly on human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) derived sensory neurons by increasing their STAT3 phosphorylation (pSTAT3) levels and expression of select pain-relevant genes. In this study, we determined that LIF is the most consequential cytokine out of the three, altering neuronal signalling, outgrowth and pain-like behaviours in in vitro and in vivo models of arthritis. Methods: Human iPSC-derived sensory neurons were stimulated with RA synovial fluid (SF) or with cytokine-treated RA synovial fibroblast conditioned media (CM) in the absence or presence of anti-cytokine antibodies. pSTAT3 and pSTAT1 levels, and gene expression patterns, were assessed by Western blot and RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq). The immortalised dorsal root ganglion (DRG)-derived cell line (HD 10.6) was assessed for LIF-induced JAK/STAT signalling in addition to neurite outgrowth assays as a functional readout of the sensory neurons. Lastly, mouse models were used to assess pain-related behaviours in vivo. Results: LIF was found to be consistently present in the SF from painful joints from individuals with inflammatory arthritis. Western blotting revealed that the addition of RA SF to iPSC-derived sensory neurons led to LIF-dependent induction of pSTAT3 and pSTAT1, while RNA-seq demonstrated that LIF alters the transcriptome of sensory neurons more prominently than IL-6 and IL-11, up-regulating signature genes related to peripheral neuron sensitization, such as TRPV1, NTRK1, BDNF, HRH1 and SCN10A. Similarly, cytokine-treated fibroblast conditioned media was shown to induce neuronal pSTAT3 and pSTAT1 and upregulate expression of BDNF, HRH1 and VGF in a LIF-dependent manner. Additionally, the immortalised dorsal root ganglion (DRG)-derived cell line (HD 10.6), which also exhibited LIF-induced pSTAT1 and pSTAT3, showed increased neurite outgrowth after axotomy when treated with LIF. Finally, in a mouse model of inflammatory arthritis, LIF was shown to be significantly increased in the affected joint. Furthermore, intraarticular injection of LIF into a healthy mouse knee resulted in increased responsiveness to painful pressure stimuli in that joint. Conclusions: Our data indicate that LIF may be a pro-algesic mediator and a possible therapeutic target to improve pain management in individuals living with inflammatory arthritis.

title: Sex shapes capillary flows and oxygen extraction in the middle-aged mouse brain
abstract: Sex differences in brain aging are well documented, but their origin within the cerebrovascular hierarchy remains unclear. Here we show that cortical blood flow is higher in female than male mice at 15 months of age, at a point when an earlier sex difference in pulsatility and resistance indices has already converged, pial vessel diameter shows no difference between sexes, and estrogen levels are similar between sexes. Using an indicator-dilution and intravascular oxygen measurements using two-photon microscopy, we found that capillary transit-time heterogeneity (CTH) scales more steeply with mean transit time in females, consistent with a passively regulated capillary network, and that this is accompanied by reduced oxygen extraction fraction (OEF) without deficit in arterial oxygen delivery. Spatial transcriptomics reveals that sex differences are organized into distinct regional programs, most prominently in white matter, where a male-associated myelin and axonogenesis signature accompanies reduced white matter volume in females. These molecular and structural differences coincide with elevated hippocampal microglial reactivity and an altered spatial search strategy in females, without any detectable differences in circulating markers of stress, blood-brain barrier integrity, or immunity. Together, these findings indicate that sex differences in the aging brain are expressed at the level of capillary flow regulation and regional tissue programs rather than through bulk cerebral blood flow alone, and that elevated blood flow in females can mask, rather than reflect, adequate tissue oxygenation.

title: A Humanized Mouse Model of DRPLA Recapitulates Epilepsy and Demonstrates Antisense Oligonucleotide-Mediated Disease Modification
abstract: Dentatorubral-pallidoluysian atrophy (DRPLA) is an ultra-rare progressive myoclonus epilepsy caused by a glutamine-coding CAG repeat expansion in atrophin-1 (ATN1). Mutant ATN1 (mATN1) expression results in symptoms that inversely correlate to CAG-expansion size: young-onset cases have the most CAG repeats and developmental delay, high-frequency treatment-resistant seizures, and early mortality. We sought to characterize the seizure susceptibility of a fully humanized ATN1 mouse expressing human mATN1 with 112 CAG repeats to then assess therapeutic antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) intervention on seizure-related outcomes. Atn1Q112/+ or wild-type (WT) mice were treated with investigational ASO targeting human, CAG-expanded, ATN1 or saline (P2 and then again at 4 weeks-old) before acute seizure testing, ataxia profiling, and chronic in vivo video-EEG recording for spontaneous seizures up to 8 weeks-old. Saline-treated Atn1Q112/+ mice were more seizure prone with early death. However, ASO administration to Atn1Q112/+ mice normalized seizure threshold, decreased ataxia, and protected against early death. Atn1Q112/+ mice exhibited spontaneous behavioral seizures recorded over 2 weeks, which were absent in ASO-treated Atn1Q112/+ and WT mice, with a specific mATN1 expression-driven decrease in delta and theta EEG frequencies. Atn1Q112/+ mice are highly seizure prone, validating this model for DRPLA epilepsy. ATN1 represents a novel epilepsy-related risk factor for therapeutic investigation.

title: Fast Generalized Longitudinal Functional Principal Components Analysis with Applications to Population-Level Neuronal Dynamics
abstract: Functional data are widely collected across many fields. One approach for modeling functional data collected across repeated measures is longitudinal functional PCA (LFPCA), which allows for the decomposition of variability at multiple levels. However, existing estimation approaches for LFPCA can be computationally demanding for large or high-dimensional datasets. Here, we propose fast generalized LFPCA, a novel estimation technique that bins data along the functional domain and fits a marginal mixed model at each bin. Simulation results show that the proposed method is orders of magnitude faster than existing techniques while achieving similar accuracy, making LFPCA scalable to datasets with more densely sampled observations and larger sample sizes. We apply the proposed technique to model neuronal firing rate data both on and off deep brain stimulation (DBS) to investigate how the intervention modulates population-level neuronal activity. Our results suggest that the vast majority of between-neuron variation can be explained by four principal components, which relate to individual differences in neuronal firing as well as the arm manipulation paradigm under study. We also find that DBS significantly increases the variability of firing activity, likely driven by increased firing from a subset of neurons in response to DBS, a novel insight not obtained in previous analyses. Code to implement the proposed method and run simulation studies is included in the supplement.

title: Vibrotactile stimulation on the upper back requires stronger vibration during goal-directed reaching but does not impede reaching performance
abstract: Vibrotactile stimulation is a promising method of biofeedback, with potential applications for ergonomic posture and balance, rehabilitation, and motor learning. These applications require balancing tactile perception with motor performance and cognitive workload. In this study, participants performed a detection task, a reaching task, and a concurrent reach-and-detect task, with vibrotactile signals delivered on the hand or upper back. Sensitivity to stimuli, motor performance, and cognitive workload were compared for each task. Sensitivity was suppressed during movement, but this suppression was greater on hand compared to the upper back. Movement time was slowed by vibration on the hand but not the upper back. Mental workload and task complexity increased for the reach-and-detect task compared to the individual tasks. We conclude that vibrotactile feedback devices worn on the upper back do not impede motor performance, with only minor tactile suppression. This could be overcome by presenting highly salient or personalized feedback.

title: Functional characterization of the 26RFa/orexin neurons of the lateral hypothalamic area reveals their key role in the control of glucose homeostasis
abstract: Defining the nature and molecular mechanisms of the neurocircuitry controlling glucose homeostasis is crucial in understanding how alterations in these pathways promote the development of obesity and type 2 diabetes. Here, we functionally characterize a population of lateral hypothalamic neurons co-expressing the anti-hyperglycemic neuropeptides 26RFa and orexin. Using complementary chemogenetic, pharmacological and genetic approaches, including mice deficient for 26RFa, orexin or both neuropeptides, we investigated the respective contribution of each signaling system to glucose homeostasis. We found that lateral hypothalamic 26RFa neurons extensively co-express orexin, defining a distinct peptidergic population with convergent anti-hyperglycemic properties. Unexpectedly, chemogenetic activation of these neurons potentiated glucose-induced hyperglycemia despite the anti-hyperglycemic properties of both neuropeptides. To understand this paradox, we examined the transcriptional responses of the 26RFa and orexin peptidergic systems and found that neuronal activation was associated with coordinated, glycemic state-dependent downregulation of both signaling systems. Furthermore, genetic loss-of-function approaches revealed distinct contributions of the two neuropeptidergic systems, with orexin signaling mediating most of the metabolic consequences of neuronal activation, whereas 26RFa signaling is required for the dynamic regulation of orexin expression. Finally, our findings provide new insights into the functional organization of lateral hypothalamic 26RFa/orexin neurons and advance our understanding of how coordinated neuropeptidergic signaling contributes to systemic glucose homeostasis.

title: An anatomy-constrained transcriptomic screen identifies a 19-gene panel with an ordered regional similarity pattern in the human somatosensory system
abstract: Neuroanatomical pathways link specialized brain regions, but whether regional transcriptomic profiles preserve relationships aligned with pathway order remains unclear. We defined candidate pathways and their available tissue representations from neuroanatomical literature, then screened 10,262 genes in the Body Index of Gene Expression (BIGE), a human microarray resource covering cells and tissues. The screen required expression across every mapped region of a route and limited single-region dominance. It identified 23 candidates in three routes with sufficient coverage; 19 met the criteria for the dorsal column-medial lemniscus (DCML) representation and formed the fixed panel. We evaluated this panel in six Allen Human Brain Atlas (AHBA) donors across three central regional representations: an aggregate of samples assigned to the cuneate and gracile nuclei (Cu/Gr), the lateral group of nuclei, ventral division, within the dorsal thalamus (DTLv), and postcentral gyrus. The regional-order contrast compared the mean similarity of the pairs adjacent in the anatomical sequence, Cu/Gr-DTLv and DTLv-postcentral gyrus, with Cu/Gr-postcentral gyrus similarity. Both adjacent-in-order correlations were positive in all six donors; the contrast was positive in five and reached a mean of T = 0.345175 (exact sign test, P = 0.109375). The panel exceeded two distributions of 50,000 gene sets generated under comparable selection constraints (P = 0.027919 and P = 0.026579). In descriptive anatomical comparisons, it ranked third among 240 combinations and first among the target and all 16 single-region substitutions. All 50,000 one-probe-per-gene analyses retained T > 0, and broad neuronal-expression contrasts were positive in medulla, thalamus, and cortex. Spatial support depended on the null model, with stronger evidence under whole-donor surrogates (P = 0.003860) than under the primary within-compartment model (P = 0.051179). These findings identify a fixed gene panel whose regional similarity is aligned with the represented central order of the DCML system and define a specific hypothesis for prospective evaluation in an independent, anatomically resolved dataset.

title: Multi-parametric spectral modeling disentangles synaptic kinetics and neural excitability from non-invasive electrophysiological recordings
abstract: Spectral modeling of electrophysiological recordings enables non-invasive characterization of neural excitability. However, current approaches rely on a single spectral index, limiting insight into the multiple biophysical processes underlying excitation-inhibition balance. Here, we introduce a biologically informed, multi-parametric spectral analysis that disentangles neural excitability and synaptic kinetics from recordings. As a proof of concept, we demonstrate that this approach captures signatures of hyperexcitability and glutamate reuptake dysfunction characteristic of Alzheimer's disease.

title: Perineuronal nets in the bed nucleus of stria terminalis mediate stress-induced anxiety behaviour in adult male mice
abstract: Anxiety disorders affect an estimated 301.4 million people globally. However, they remain among the most challenging conditions to treat, with only around half of patients reporting a 50% or greater reduction in their symptoms. The discovery of novel and more effective treatments therefore requires a better understanding of the underlying mechanisms of anxiety at both the circuit and cellular levels. Stress induces aberrant changes in neuronal plasticity across brain regions within the anxiety circuitry including the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BNST). One mechanism through which synaptic plasticity is regulated is the organisation of perineuronal nets (PNNs), specialised extracellular matrix structures that are highly sensitive to stress. In rodent models, stress is associated with a reduction in PNN number and/or decreased Wisteria floribunda Agglutinin (WFA) labelling in limbic areas. However, the development of PNNs within the BNST and their role in the stress responsiveness remain largely unknown. In the current study we investigated the spatiotemporal development of PNNs within the BNST of male mice, where they first appear at P30 and continue to mature into adulthood, reaching their highest expression at P210 and specifically within the anteromedial BNST. We further showed that stress-induced anxiety is associated with a reduction in PNN number and significant changes to PNN fine structure including increased leakiness in the anteromedial BNST. Most importantly, enzymatic removal of PNNs by chondroitinase ABC in the mouse anteromedial BNST exacerbated behavioural responses to acute stress as demonstrated by increased anxiety-like behaviour. Collectively, these results highlight an indispensable role for PNNs within the anteromedial BNST in mediating a healthy emotional response to psychosocial stress.

title: Longitudinal associations between task-control network functioning, cognition, and the environment in early adolescence
abstract: Neural maturation in the "task-control" frontoparietal and dorsal attention networks is thought to support the development of adolescents' cognitive and adaptive functioning. Further, theory suggests that family and neighborhood contexts shape brain network development. Yet, few longitudinal studies have examined the co-development of brain network mechanisms with cognitive and adaptive functioning or with environmental factors that could shape the maturation of these mechanisms. The present study addressed these gaps. We used longitudinal data spanning late childhood (Mage=10 years) to early adolescence (Mage=12) from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study (n=4862). Stable and construct-valid neural signatures of task-control network functioning were estimated using longitudinal bifactor modeling of neural responses to cognitive demand during the n-back task. Multivariate latent change-score models were used to examine co-development of this signature with cognitive efficiency (drift rate from the diffusion model), teacher-reported attention problems, family conflict, and neighborhood safety. Models accounted for baseline family income. Robust reciprocal relations between task-control activation and cognitive efficiency were identified and the latent change scores for efficiency and task-control activation were positively correlated. Similar reciprocal associations were observed between cognitive efficiency and attention problems. Baseline family income predicted the rate of change in task-control network functioning. This study demonstrates that task-control network functioning co-develops with cognition, which in turn supports attentional functioning development across early adolescence. Further, findings highlight the utility of this neural signature of task-control network functioning for understanding the neural basis of cognitive development and the mechanisms through which environmental experiences shape brain and behavior.

title: Long-Range Glutamatergic Projections Target Hippocampal Cajal-Retzius Cells Through Atypical Receptor Signaling
abstract: Cajal-Retzius (CR) cells are a population of early-born, transient neurons that serve an indispensable role during embryonic brain development. Postnatally, most CR cells undergo programmed cell-death, except in a few areas, including the hippocampus, where they persist until adulthood. The hippocampal population of CR (hCR) cells have previously been implicated in receiving and facilitating ingrowth of entorhinal afferents and the establishment of the hippocampal circuit. Nevertheless, only local GABAergic synaptic input has been demonstrated onto hCR cells before. Through transsynaptic rabies tracing we show that hCR cells receive input for at least seven extrahippocampal areas, all putative glutamatergic populations, even though CR cell spontaneous activity is speculated to be exclusively mediated through GABAergic action. Here, we show that a portion of CR cell spontaneous activity is strychnine-sensitive, and that glutamatergic fibers from entorhinal cortex layer II apposition themselves in physiological distance (<300 nm) to glycinergic receptors on hCR cells. We propose that hCR cells guide several, if not all, afferents terminating in stratum lacunosum moleculare and the outer molecular layer in the hippocampus. These findings shine new light on how hCR cells might facilitate hippocampal maturation.
